8e6b5d85-0b53-580f-9520-6c33463231d5.title: Integrating Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Some Manipulations

e-386.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\textrm{d}x = \arcsin (x) + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-387.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+x^2}\textrm{d}x = \arctan{x} + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3890.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}} \, \textrm dx = \textrm{arcsec} \, x.
$$

Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}-2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\text{arcsec}\,(x)-2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =5\text{arcsec}\,(x)-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-388.knowledge_point: Integrating Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Some Manipulations
e-388.worked_solution:
This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+2}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1+1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \textrm dx = \arctan(x),
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int 1\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating term by term, ∫8x dx = 4x² and ∫1/√(1−x²) dx = arcsin(x). Thus the integral is 4x²−arcsin(x)+C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (8x-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})\text{d}x & =\int 8x\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\int x\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{2}-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

∫(31−x2−6x2)dx=

a
arctan⁡x−2x3+C
b
 arcsec x+4x3+C
c
3 arcsec x−4x+C
d
3arcsin⁡x+3x+C
e
3arcsin⁡x−2x3+C

decision.explanation: Integrating term by term gives 3 arcsin(x) for 3/√(1−x²) and −2x³ for −6x². Thus option e is correct.

∫11−x2dx=arcsin⁡x+C.

∫(31−x2−6x2)dx=∫31−x2dx−∫6x2dx=3∫11−x2dx−6∫x2dx=3arcsin⁡x−6⋅x33+C=3arcsin⁡x−2x3+C.

Question 7
?

∫(41+x2−sin⁡x)dx=

a
4 arcsec x−tan⁡x+C
b
4arctan⁡x+cos⁡x+C
c
2arctan⁡x−cos⁡x+C
d
2arcsin⁡x+sin⁡x+C
e
4arctan⁡x−tan⁡x+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating 4/(1+x²) gives 4 arctan(x), and integrating −sin(x) gives cos(x). Therefore option b is correct.

Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that ∫11+x2dx=arctan⁡x+C.

Therefore, we have

∫(41+x2−sin⁡x)dx=∫41+x2dx−∫sin⁡xdx=4∫11+x2dx−∫sin⁡xdx=4arctan⁡x−(−cos⁡x)+C=4arctan⁡x+cos⁡x+C.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+\frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}})\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int x\,\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The derivative of arcsec(y) is 1/(|y|√(y²−1)). Multiplying its antiderivative by 2 gives 2 arcsec(y)+C, so option c is correct.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \frac{1}{|y|\sqrt{{y}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}y=\text{arcsec}\,y.
$$

Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|y|\sqrt{{y}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}y & =2\int \frac{1}{|y|\sqrt{{y}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\text{ arcsec }y+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

∫(5sin⁡x+4|x|x2−1)dx=

a
5sec⁡x−4 arcsec x+C
b
5cos⁡x+4 arcsec x+C
c
−5sec⁡x−4 arcsin x+C
d
−5cos⁡x+4 arcsec x+C
e
−5cos⁡x+4 arcsin x+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating term by term, 5 sin(x) gives −5 cos(x), and 4/(|x|√(x²−1)) gives 4 arcsec(x). Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=\text{arcsec}\,x.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{4}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}})\text{d}x & =\int 5\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+4\text{ arcsec }x+C \\  & =-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\text{ arcsec }x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that ∫1|x|x2−1dx=arcsecx.

Therefore, we have

∫(5sin⁡x+4|x|x2−1)dx=∫5sin⁡xdx+∫4|x|x2−1dx=5∫sin⁡xdx+4∫1|x|x2−1dx=5(−cos⁡x)+4 arcsec x+C=−5cos⁡x+4 arcsec x+C.

content.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=\text{arcsec}\,x.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{4}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}})\text{d}x & =\int 5\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+4\text{ arcsec }x+C \\  & =-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\text{ arcsec }x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Rewrite (x²+6)/(x²+1) as 1+5/(x²+1). Integrating gives x+5 arctan(x)+C, so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-1+6}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)+5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =1+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+\int \frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+5\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+5\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}

content.worked_solution:
This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-1+6}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)+5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =1+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+\int \frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+5\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+5\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{5{x}^{2}+5-5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{5({x}^{2}+1)-5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{5({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}-\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{5\cancel{({x}^{2}+1)}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}-\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =5-\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (5-\frac{5}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5x-5\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)+1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{2x\cancel{({x}^{2}+1)}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

f′(x)=2x3+2x+1x2+1=2x(x2+1)+1x2+1=2x(x2+1)x2+1+1x2+1=2x+1x2+1

Remembering that ∫11+x2dx=arctan⁡x+C, we can now calculate the integral and get

f(x)=∫f′(x)dx=∫(2x+1x2+1)dx=2∫xdx+∫1x2+1dx=2⋅x22+arctan⁡x+C=x2+arctan⁡x+C.

This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{4{x}^{2}+4-4}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{4({x}^{2}+1)-4}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{4({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{4\cancel{({x}^{2}+1)}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =4-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

4x2x2+1=4x2+4−4x2+1=4(x2+1)−4x2+1=4(x2+1)x2+1−4x2+1=4(x2+1)x2+1−4x2+1=4−4x2+1

Remembering that ∫1x2+1dx=arctan⁡x, we can now calculate the integral and get
